title: Amazon EventBridge API Destination to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
description: Invoke an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime agent directly from Amazon EventBridge without AWS Lambda glue code, using an API Destination with Amazon Cognito M2M OAuth.

introBox.headline: How it works
text: This pattern shows event-driven invocation of an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime agent with no AWS Lambda function in the path and no glue code. An Amazon EventBridge rule on a custom event bus matches events and delivers them straight to the runtime through an API Destination. The AWS CDK stack is self-contained: it builds and deploys the AgentCore Runtime from a bundled agent container image alongside the EventBridge plumbing, so a single cdk deploy gives you a working, testable pattern.

The EventBridge Connection authenticates with Amazon Cognito machine-to-machine (M2M) OAuth: it fetches an access token from the Cognito user pool token endpoint using the client_credentials grant and attaches it as a Bearer token. The AgentCore Runtime validates that JWT through its inbound identity (customJwtAuthorizer), which the stack wires to the same Cognito user pool and app client at creation time, so there is no manual post-deploy step.

Because API Destinations enforce a hard 5-second response timeout and agent reasoning takes longer, the agent entrypoint acknowledges the request immediately and processes the event in the background. The background work is registered with the AgentCore SDK @app.async_task decorator, so the runtime reports HealthyBusy and keeps the session alive until the agent finishes.

The endpoint URL uses the agent runtime ID plus an accountId query parameter instead of a URL-encoded ARN, because API Destinations automatically decode percent-encoded sequences in the target URL and would otherwise corrupt the ARN's colons and slashes.

Deliveries that fail after three retries land in an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue. The DLQ captures delivery failures only (401/403, 5xx, timeouts): once the runtime has acknowledged, a failure in the background agent work is written to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and is not retried or sent to the DLQ. Delivery is at-least-once and the pattern does no deduplication, so the rule forwards the EventBridge event ID for use as an idempotency key.

These are deliberate omissions to keep the pattern minimal. For production, report each background outcome durably (a follow-up EventBridge event, an Amazon DynamoDB record, or an AWS Step Functions task-token callback), check the event ID against an idempotency store before side effects, and add an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the DLQ's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric.

IAM permissions follow least privilege: the AgentCore Runtime execution role grants only ecr:BatchGetImage and ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer on the specific ECR repository, scoped Amazon CloudWatch Logs and AWS X-Ray permissions, and bedrock:InvokeModel limited to foundation models and inference profiles. The EventBridge rule's target role has only events:InvokeApiDestination on the specific API Destination, and the SQS dead-letter queue enforces SSL in transit.

testing.headline: Testing
text: Publish a test event to the custom bus (the EventBusName output, agentcore-events): aws events put-events --entries '[{"EventBusName":"agentcore-events","Source":"demo.orders","DetailType":"OrderCreated","Detail":"{\"orderId\":\"12345\",\"prompt\":\"Summarize this order and flag any anomalies.\"}"}]'
Check the AgentCore Runtime's Amazon CloudWatch Logs (/aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/<AgentRuntimeId>-DEFAULT) to see the event arrive and the background processing run.
Confirm the connection is usable: aws events describe-connection --name agentcore-cognito-oauth should show AUTHORIZED.
If delivery fails after retries, inspect the DLQ: aws sqs receive-message --queue-url .
